newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Pressure mounts on Austrian chancellor to resign.
newsitem.headline: Pressure mounts on Austrian chancellor to resign.

text.p: Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky's leadership faced scrutiny on Thursday as former allies questioned his ability to turn Social Democrat fortunes around after a dismal showing in a European Parliament election.
Senior party members and normally sympathetic union bosses raised the spectre of a change in the party leadership after 10 years of continuity accompanied by a spectacular decline in voter support.

"The European election result was a catastrophe. It is not enough to undertake a reform of party policy, heads must role at the very top," Hannes Androsch, a former Social Democrat finance minister and vice chancellor, said.

The Social Democrats slumped to their lowest level of popularity since 1918 in Sunday's European parliamentary vote, scoring just 29.1 percent. When Vranitzky became chancellor in 1986 his party had the backing of almost half the electorate.
"Vranitzky must take responsibility...and draw the necessary conclusions," Androsch, a former protege of revered postwar chancellor Bruno Kreisky, added.
On Sunday, the Social Democrats fell behind junior coalition partners the People's Party for the first time in 30 years and finished just 60,000 votes ahead of Joerg Haider's far-right Freedom Party.

Vranitzky, Europe's longest serving government leader after Chancellor Helmut Kohl of Germany, has shrugged off the humiliation and insisted he will lead his party into the next general election, scheduled for 1999.

But the party faithful have begun to doubt his ability to steer the Social Democratic Party out of the darkest period in its democratic history and some have accused him of losing touch with the grass roots.
"New demands will be made on the party leadership, demands that Vranitzky may well not be able to meet," said Karl Heinz Herper, regional manager of the Styria Social Democrats.
"We need a completely "new Vranitzky' but I can't see the old one changing his stripes."

Influential union boss Hans Sallmutter forecast rising tensions in the ruling coalition as the Social Democrats sought to draw a clear line between themselves and the conservative People's Party in a bid to win back working class voters lost to Haider's populist movement.
"There will be some emotional discussions in the government and one must bear in mind that the next general election could come before 1999," Sallmutter said.
"The Social Democratic Party must review its policies ...After that it has to decide on a leadership team that will bring it success," he added.
Austrian media have also sensed that Vranitzky's grip on the reins of government is loosening and have begun the search for a successor.
Under the headline "Arrivederci, Vranz" weekly current affairs magazine news forecast there would be a change at the chancellery within 12 months.
It rated Finance Minister Viktor Klima the top candidate, followed closely by Vienna mayor Michael Haeupl and Androsch.
"Talk about reform is not enough. If we don't act we face difficult times ahead," said party manager Brigitte Ederer.
